messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Psychologist
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 61

He is 37, an African man who lives alone and works as a psychologist in a busy outpatient clinic. By the time he speaks about what happened, he does so with the careful, measured tone he uses with his own patients, as if precision might keep him from being overwhelmed. But when he tells the story in order, it becomes clear how much of his life is organized around not feeling what began one night two years earlier.

At the time, he is finishing a professional conference in another city. He remembers being tired, pleased with how his presentation had gone, and a little lonely in the anonymous comfort of the hotel. He goes out for one drink with a small group of attendees. Later, when the group breaks up, one man he has spoken with casually offers to walk with him part of the way back. He remembers trying to be polite, not wanting to appear suspicious. In his account, the details sharpen suddenly at the point where the evening turns. The man insists on coming upstairs “just for a minute.” He says no more than once, then laughs awkwardly, trying to smooth things over. What follows is a blur of pressure, disbelief, and then unmistakable force.

He says that his clearest memory is not of fighting, but of freezing. He can still feel the paralysis of it, the split second in which his mind tells him this cannot be happening to him, not here, not like this. He remembers staring at the patterned hotel carpet afterward, noticing one thread pulled loose, and feeling a detached shame at how ordinary the room looks. He showers for a long time. He throws away his clothes. He does not call the police. He does not tell anyone. On the train home he sits rigidly upright, unable to tolerate the brush of another passenger’s arm, while a voice in his head repeats that he should have prevented it, should have seen it coming, should have fought harder.

In the weeks afterward, he returns to work almost immediately. He listens to patients describe panic, grief, and violation, and finds himself gripping his pen so tightly that his hand aches. He becomes preoccupied with the idea that someone will notice a change in him. He worries that if he lets his attention drift, he will miss a risk cue, fail a patient, expose himself as weak. At night he sleeps in fragments. When sleep does come, he wakes with his heart racing, the hotel room returning in flashes: the smell of cologne, the weight pinning him down, the humiliating disbelief. Sometimes he startles awake already standing, having knocked over a bedside lamp in the dark.

He avoids the city where the conference took place, then gradually avoids all professional travel. He declines invitations, telling colleagues he is overextended. He stops going out socially after evening events because he cannot bear the calculation of who is standing too close, who is watching, how quickly he can leave. Dating, which had already felt complicated, disappears from his life entirely. If someone expresses interest, he becomes tense and distant. Touch feels dangerous because it is so unpredictable; even a friendly hand on his shoulder in the clinic can flood him with heat and nausea.

What troubles him especially is the way the assault infiltrates his work. He had built his identity around being calm in crisis, someone who can help others contain what feels unbearable. Now, in sessions with trauma survivors, he sometimes hears one phrase that catches against his own memory and feels himself disappear from the room for a second or two. He knows the mechanics of dissociation; knowing does not stop it. He begins arranging his office with unusual care, keeping his chair angled toward the door, checking the hallway before his last appointment, staying late to avoid sharing the elevator. He tells himself these are sensible precautions, but he also knows they are part of a life that has narrowed.

He carries intense shame about being raped as a man. He has spent much of his career encouraging patients to challenge self-blame, yet he finds his own mind merciless. He worries about cultural expectations of masculinity, about how this story would be heard in his family, about whether anyone would subtly disbelieve him. Sometimes he catches himself minimizing it—calling it “the incident,” as if language can reduce its force. Other times anger breaks through unexpectedly: at the man who assaulted him, at the hotel staff who said good morning the next day and noticed nothing, at himself for continuing to perform competence.

Now, even in ordinary life, his body behaves as though the danger is current. He scans entrances in restaurants, sits with his back to walls, and keeps conversations brief with unfamiliar men. He drinks more on weekends than he used to, not enough to miss work, but enough to blunt the edge of evening. He feels cut off from people and then ashamed of his isolation. He says he is tired of living in anticipation of being trapped again. What he wants most is simple and, to him, almost unimaginable: to move through a room without first calculating escape.
